passage:
Elif turned her phone face down on the café table in Uppsala and let it buzz. Oskar again. Third call.
They had argued about his weekend trip with the climbing club. He hadn't asked before booking it, and she had wanted to say it made her feel like an afterthought, but the words stuck. Arguing out loud with Oskar always ended with her crying and him staying calm. Silence was easier. Silence she could win.
So for two days she read his messages and didn't answer. Are you okay? Did I do something? I'll cancel if you want.
That last one gave her a small, hot flicker of satisfaction. Then it faded, and something else crept in. He wasn't learning why she was hurt. He was only learning to fear her quiet.
She picked up the phone and began, slowly, to type the sentence she had swallowed.

qa.q: Where was Elif when she let the phone buzz?
qa.a: She was at a café table in Uppsala.

qa.q: What did Elif feel when Oskar offered to cancel?
qa.a: She felt a small, hot flicker of satisfaction, then unease as she saw he was only learning to fear her quiet.

qa.q: What turning point is Elif reaching when she starts to type?
qa.a: She chooses to say the swallowed sentence, that she felt like an afterthought, instead of using silence to make Oskar give in, which gives them a real problem to solve.

qa.q: How might the two days of silence feel to Oskar?
qa.a: He likely felt anxious and confused, guessing what he did wrong and ready to give up his trip just to end the silence.

grounding: A young woman goes silent after an argument, enjoys the power when Oskar pleads, then sees the silence punishes him instead of explaining her hurt.

passage:
For five days Naveen did not say a word to Vasudha in the fest committee room. He answered her questions by speaking to the room: "Someone tell the sound people it's four o'clock." He sat with his back half-turned.
It had started when she overruled his stage plan in front of the whole committee. He could have argued, but she was quicker with words, and losing twice in public felt unbearable. Silence felt like the one place he couldn't lose.
On Friday Vasudha stopped at his desk, eyes tired. "I'm sorry, okay? For whatever I did. Can we please go back to normal?"
Naveen had waited all week for this. He nodded, cool, and felt the win.
Walking back to the hostel, he kept replaying her face. She hadn't agreed with him. She had only given up. Nothing about the stage was settled; she had simply been made to pay.

qa.q: How long did Naveen avoid speaking to Vasudha?
qa.a: He did not say a word to Vasudha for five days in the fest committee room.

qa.q: Why did silence feel safer to Naveen than arguing?
qa.a: Vasudha was quicker with words and he feared losing twice in public, so silence felt like the one place he couldn't lose.

qa.q: What could Naveen have done after being overruled in the meeting?
qa.a: He could have said he felt embarrassed and asked for a separate talk about his stage plan, instead of withdrawing to make her plead.

qa.q: What was the week of silence like for Vasudha?
qa.a: She was worn down and tired, apologising for whatever she did without knowing her fault, just to end the cold treatment.

grounding: A young man goes silent for a week after being overruled, waits for Vasudha to plead, and realises the apology he won settled nothing.

passage:
After the argument in a Kolkata café about her college trip to Manali, Kunal stopped replying to Madhuri. He saw her messages come in, one by one: "Can we talk?" "I'm sorry if I upset you." "Please say something."
He read them all and put the phone face down. A small, hard satisfaction settled in his chest. She'd come round. She'd cancel the trip. He didn't have to argue. He just had to wait.
On the second day she sent, "Okay, I won't go." He felt a rush of power. Then, strangely, it curdled. He pictured her crying on her bed, cancelling something she'd saved for all year, just to make his silence stop.
He hadn't protected anything. He'd just punished her until she gave in.
Kunal picked up the phone. "I'm sorry. I went silent to get my way. Go to Manali. Can we talk tonight?"

qa.q: Where was Madhuri's college trip?
qa.a: To Manali.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel as he read her messages and waited?
qa.a: Kunal felt a hard satisfaction and a sense of power, expecting his silence to make her give in without him having to argue.

qa.q: What did Kunal do once he saw what his silence was doing?
qa.a: He apologised, named that he went silent to get his way, told her to go, and asked to talk that night.

qa.q: How did Madhuri feel during the two days of silence?
qa.a: Madhuri felt anxious and desperate, sending messages and finally cancelling the trip just to make the silence stop.

grounding: It shows a young adult using silence after a disagreement to make his partner give in, and recognising it as punishment rather than protection.

passage:
"You haven't said a word to Sudha in three days," Jyoti's cousin Neel said, watching her scroll on the hostel bed.
"She knows why."
"Because she didn't lend you her notes?"
"Because she said no. In front of everyone."
"So talk to her."
"Why should I? She'll come to me. She always does."
Neel frowned. "So this is a strategy."
Jyoti shrugged. "Silence works. She'll say sorry and give me the notes. I don't have to fight."
"Jyoti, that's not you being calm. That's you punishing her until she gives up."
"It's easier than arguing."
"Easier for you. What about her?"
Jyoti stopped scrolling. Sudha had been eating alone in the mess, eyes red. Jyoti had noticed and felt… powerful. Now, hearing it said aloud, that feeling tasted bad.
"She was allowed to say no," Jyoti said quietly.
"Yeah. She was."

qa.q: How many days had Jyoti not spoken to Sudha?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What did Jyoti feel when she noticed Sudha eating alone?
qa.a: Jyoti felt powerful at first, and then, hearing Neel, that feeling turned bad and uncomfortable.

qa.q: What did Neel help Jyoti see?
qa.a: Neel helped her see that her silence was not calm but a way to punish Sudha until she gave in, and that Sudha was allowed to say no.

qa.q: How was Sudha affected by the silence?
qa.a: Sudha felt hurt and alone, eating by herself in the mess with red eyes.

grounding: It shows a young adult using silence to make a flatmate give in, feeling powerful, until a cousin names it as punishment.

passage:
I'm Nirmala, and I used to be very good at silence.
When my brother Arnab refused to lend me his scooter for a trip in second year, I stopped speaking to him. Not a word at breakfast, not a word at dinner, for five days. I moved my plate when he sat down. I answered Amma, never him.
I told myself I was just calm. Mature, even. I wasn't shouting. But I knew exactly what I was doing. I was waiting for him to crack. Words felt risky: he might argue back, he might be right. Silence felt safe and strong.
On day five he knocked on my door with the keys. His eyes were red. "Take it. Just talk to me."
I took the keys. And I felt terrible. I had won, and he looked like someone who'd been hit.
I don't do that anymore. When I'm angry now, I say so.

qa.q: For how many days did Nirmala not speak to Arnab?
qa.a: For five days.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala choose silence instead of words?
qa.a: Nirmala felt that words were risky, since Arnab might argue or be right, while silence felt safe and powerful.

qa.q: What does Nirmala do differently now?
qa.a: When angry, Nirmala now says so directly instead of using silence to punish.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel by day five?
qa.a: Arnab felt hurt and worn down, with red eyes, giving in just to make Nirmala talk to him.

grounding: A young adult recalls using silence to punish a brother until he gave in, feeling powerful while words felt risky.

passage:
Coach's note, university badminton squad, Friday.
Vidya and Jatin (mixed doubles) disagreed on Monday about who covers the back court. Since then Vidya has not spoken to Jatin at all: no eye contact, turning away at drinks breaks, answering his questions only through me. Jatin has apologised twice, each time more anxiously; on Wednesday he offered to switch to the front court "if that fixes it". Vidya looked satisfied, but stayed silent.
After practice today I asked Vidya to stay back and asked what the silence was doing for her. She took a long time, then said, "When I stop talking, he comes round. When I argue, I lose." She seemed surprised to hear herself say it.
We agreed she will tell Jatin what she actually wants on court, in words, by Monday. I will sit in if both want. I will check in with Jatin separately too.

qa.q: What did Jatin offer on Wednesday?
qa.a: He offered to switch to the front court if that fixes it.

qa.q: What did Vidya's answer reveal about her silence?
qa.a: Vidya seemed to feel powerless in arguments and in control when silent; she looked surprised, even uneasy, hearing herself say it.

qa.q: How did the coach respond, and why does it help?
qa.a: The coach asked Vidya privately what the silence was doing, then agreed a plan for her to state her wishes in words by Monday, with an offer to sit in and a separate check on Jatin.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin under the silence?
qa.a: Jatin seems anxious and keeps apologising, even offering to change position, just to make the silence end.

grounding: Shows a young adult going silent after a disagreement so the other pleads and gives in, using silence as power when arguing felt risky.
